modules.title: Introduction to Miro
modules.content:
## The Death of the Physical Whiteboard

Imagine you are leading a brainstorming session with four colleagues. Two are in the office with you, one is working from a home office three states away, and another is dialing in from a different time zone entirely. 

In a traditional setting, you would stand at a physical whiteboard, marker in hand, while the remote team members watched a grainy webcam feed of your back. They would struggle to see the handwriting, feel disconnected from the process, and rely on you to "scribe" every single one of their ideas. The moment the meeting ended, someone would have to take a photo of the board—which would inevitably get buried in an email thread—and manually transcribe those notes into a document.

This is where a **Virtual Whiteboarding Tool** changes the game. 

A virtual whiteboard is a digital space that mimics the experience of a physical board but removes the limitations of geography and physical space. Instead of a wall in a conference room, you have a shared digital environment where everyone can draw, write, and move elements simultaneously. It transforms a meeting from a "presentation" (one person talking, others listening) into a "co-creation" (everyone contributing in real-time).

Miro is one of the industry leaders in this space. At its core, Miro provides an **Infinite Canvas**—a digital workspace that has no edges. Unlike a PowerPoint slide or a Word document, which has a fixed page size, a Miro board expands in every direction as you add content. You can zoom out to see a high-level map of a project or zoom in to read a single sticky note.

## Getting Started: Creating Your Account

Before you can begin collaborating, you need to establish your digital presence in Miro. Because Miro is a cloud-based platform, you do not need to install heavy software to get started; it runs directly in your web browser, though a desktop app is available for a more streamlined experience.

### Step-by-Step Account Setup

1. **Visit the Sign-Up Page:** Navigate to Miro.com and select "Sign up for free."
2. **Choose Your Authentication:** You can create an account using a professional email address or use **Single Sign-On (SSO)**. SSO allows you to link your account to an existing provider like Google, Slack, or Microsoft, which removes the need to remember a new password.
3. **Define Your Role:** Miro will ask a few onboarding questions about your role (e.g., Project Manager, Designer, Educator) and your primary goals. While these are optional, they help Miro suggest relevant templates when you first enter the platform.
4. **Verify Your Email:** Check your inbox for a verification link to activate your account.

### Configuring Your Profile

Once you are logged in, it is important to configure your profile to ensure your collaborators know who is contributing.

*   **Profile Picture:** In a virtual space, a photo is your "digital face." Without one, you appear as a generic colored circle with an initial. Adding a clear headshot makes the collaboration feel more human.
*   **Display Name:** Ensure your name is entered correctly. This name will appear next to every sticky note or line you create, providing an automatic audit trail of who contributed which idea.

## Navigating the Miro Dashboard

When you first log in, you aren't placed directly onto a canvas. Instead, you land on the **Dashboard**. Think of the dashboard as your "home base" or a digital filing cabinet where all your work is organized.

### Understanding the Dashboard Layout

The dashboard is designed to give you a bird's-eye view of your current projects. The primary elements you will encounter include:

*   **The Sidebar:** This is your main navigation menu. It allows you to switch between your personal boards, team projects, and integrated apps.
*   **The Board Gallery:** This is the central area where your boards appear as thumbnails. You can quickly see a preview of the content on each board without having to open them.
*   **The "Create New Board" Button:** Usually located prominently in the top right or center, this is the starting point for every new project.
*   **Search Bar:** As your library of boards grows, the search bar becomes essential for finding specific projects by name.

### Organizing with Teams

Miro organizes work around the concept of **Teams**. A team is a shared space where multiple users can access a collection of boards. 

When you create a free account, Miro automatically creates a "Default Team" for you. If you join a company that already uses Miro, you will likely be invited to an existing team. This allows the organization to maintain a centralized library of knowledge rather than having boards scattered across individual private accounts.

## Creating Your First Board

Now that you are familiar with the dashboard, it is time to move from the "filing cabinet" to the "workspace."

### Launching the Board

Click the **(+) New Board** button on your dashboard. Miro will generate a fresh, blank infinite canvas. At first, it may look like a vast, empty grey or white void. This is intentional. 

### Initial Configuration

Before you start adding content, there are two critical settings to consider:

1.  **Board Naming:** By default, your board will be titled "Untitled." Click on the title at the top left of the screen to give it a descriptive name (e.g., "Q4 Marketing Brainstorm" or "Product Roadmap 2024"). This prevents the "Untitled 1, Untitled 2" confusion on your dashboard.
2.  **Share Settings:** In the top right corner, you will see a **Share** button. This is where you control who can see your work. You can keep the board private, invite specific people via email, or create a shareable link.

## Understanding Plan Tiers: Free vs. Paid

Miro uses a "Freemium" model. This means the core functionality of the tool is available for free, but advanced features and higher limits are locked behind paid subscriptions. Understanding these differences prevents frustration when you hit a limit mid-project.

### The Free Plan
The Free plan is ideal for individuals or small teams testing the waters. Its primary characteristics include:
*   **Limited Editable Boards:** You generally get three editable boards. Once you reach this limit, you must either delete a board or convert an old one to "view-only" to make room for a new one.
*   **Unlimited Visitors:** You can invite people to view or edit your board via a link, but they aren't formal "team members."
*   **Basic Toolset:** You have access to the core tools (sticky notes, shapes, connectors).

### Paid Plans (Starter and Business)
Paid plans are designed for professional teams who require scale, security, and advanced organization. Key upgrades include:
*   **Unlimited Boards:** You no longer have to delete old work to start new projects.
*   **Private Boards:** On the free plan, all boards within a team are visible to all team members. Paid plans allow you to create private boards that only you (and those you specifically invite) can see.
*   **Advanced Permissions:** You can set granular controls, such as allowing someone to view a board but preventing them from moving any elements.
*   **Enhanced Security:** Enterprise-level features like SSO (Single Sign-On) and advanced audit logs are available in the higher tiers.

### Summary Comparison Table

| Feature | Free Plan | Paid Plans |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Number of Boards** | Limited (usually 3) | Unlimited |
| **Board Privacy** | All team boards are public | Private boards available |
| **Collaboration** | Public links/Visitors | Full team management |
| **Advanced Tools** | Basic toolset | Full feature set (e.g., Voting, Timer) |

## Scenario: The First-Timer's Workflow

To tie these concepts together, let's look at a realistic scenario.

**The User:** Sarah, a Project Manager who has never used a virtual whiteboard.
**The Goal:** Organize a kickoff meeting for a new website redesign.

1.  **Setup:** Sarah signs up for a Miro account using her company's Google SSO. She uploads a professional photo so her team recognizes her on the canvas.
2.  **Creation:** She goes to her Dashboard and clicks "New Board." She immediately renames it "Website Redesign Kickoff" so it's easy to find later.
3.  **Planning:** Sarah realizes she is on the Free plan. She knows she has three boards available, so she decides to use one single, massive board for the entire project—leveraging the **Infinite Canvas**—rather than creating separate boards for "Research," "Ideation," and "Planning."
4.  **Invitation:** She clicks the **Share** button and sends an invite link to her three designers and two developers. Because she is on the Free plan, she invites them as "Visitors" so they can jump in and start contributing without needing to manage complex team permissions.

By following this flow, Sarah has moved from "zero" to a "collaborative environment" in less than ten minutes.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Virtual Whiteboarding** replaces physical boards with a digital, shared space that enables real-time, remote co-creation.
*   The **Infinite Canvas** is the core of Miro; it is a workspace without boundaries that allows you to scale your ideas in any direction.
*   The **Dashboard** serves as the central hub for organizing and accessing your boards via Teams.
*   **Account Setup** should include a profile picture and clear display name to facilitate human-centric collaboration.
*   **Plan Tiers** differ primarily in the number of editable boards and the level of privacy/permission control available.

modules.title: Navigating the Infinite Canvas
modules.content:
## The "Where Am I?" Moment

Imagine you’ve just joined a project board that has been active for six months. You enter the screen and see a tiny cluster of sticky notes in the center, but as you zoom out, you realize the board stretches for miles in every direction. To the north is a massive product roadmap; to the east is a messy brainstorming graveyard; to the south is a polished client presentation. 

For a beginner, the **Infinite Canvas** can feel less like a tool and more like a void. Without a map, it is incredibly easy to "get lost in the white," scrolling into an empty area of the board and forgetting how to get back to your team.

Mastering navigation is the difference between feeling overwhelmed by the scale of Miro and feeling empowered by it. Before you add a single sticky note or draw a line, you must first learn how to move.

## Mastering Pan and Zoom

In a traditional document, you move linearly (up and down). In Miro, you move in two dimensions (X and Y axes) and one depth dimension (Zoom).

### Panning: Moving Across the Canvas
**Panning** is the act of sliding your view across the board without changing how close or far away you are from the content. Think of it like sliding a piece of paper across a desk.

There are three primary ways to pan:
1.  **The Right-Click Drag:** Hold down the right mouse button and move your cursor in any direction. This is the most efficient way to move quickly across large distances.
2.  **The Spacebar Shortcut:** Hold the **Spacebar** on your keyboard. While holding it, your cursor transforms into a hand icon. You can now click and drag with your left mouse button to move the board.
3.  **The Navigation HUD:** In the bottom right corner of your screen, you will see a small directional pad (arrows). Clicking these will nudge your view in that specific direction.

### Zooming: Changing Your Perspective
**Zooming** allows you to switch between a "bird's-eye view" (seeing the entire project architecture) and a "worm's-eye view" (reading the fine print on a single sticky note).

*   **The Mouse Wheel:** Scrolling up zooms in; scrolling down zooms out.
*   **The Keyboard Shortcuts:** Use the **(+)** and **(-)** keys for incremental zooming.
*   **The Zoom Percentage:** In the bottom right corner, you will see a percentage (e.g., 100%). You can click this to select a specific zoom level or click "Fit to screen" to instantly see all the content currently on your board.

**Pro Tip:** If you ever find yourself staring at a blank white screen and can't find your work, simply press **Shift + 1**. This shortcut zooms the view to fit all existing content on the board, instantly bringing your work back into sight.

## Using the Minimap for Orientation

When a board becomes truly massive, panning and zooming can feel like wandering through a fog. You know the "Product Roadmap" is somewhere to the left, but you aren't sure how far. This is where the **Minimap** becomes essential.

The Minimap is a scaled-down, thumbnail version of your entire board, located in the bottom right corner of the interface. 

### How to interact with the Minimap:
*   **Visual Orientation:** The Minimap shows a red rectangular border. This border represents the specific area of the board you are currently seeing on your main screen.
*   **The "Jump" Technique:** Instead of panning across a vast empty space, you can click anywhere inside the Minimap. This will instantly teleport your main view to that specific location on the canvas.
*   **Expanding the Map:** If the Minimap is too small to be useful, you can click the expand icon to make it larger, providing a clearer view of the board's overall layout.

## Organizing the Chaos with Frames

If the Infinite Canvas is the land, **Frames** are the fences and street signs. Without frames, a board is just a collection of floating objects. With frames, a board becomes a structured presentation or a guided journey.

A **Frame** is a defined boundary that groups a set of objects together. Think of a frame as a "slide" within the infinite canvas.

### Creating Frames
To create a frame, select the Frame tool from the left-hand toolbar. You can then click and drag to draw a box around your content. Anything inside that box is now "contained" within that frame.

### Why Frames are Essential for Navigation:
1.  **The Frame Panel:** On the left side of the screen, you can open the Frames panel. This lists every frame on the board. Clicking a frame name in this list acts as a hyperlink, instantly zooming you to that specific section.
2.  **Logical Grouping:** Frames allow you to label sections (e.g., "Week 1 Brainstorm," "Final Approvals," "Research Data"), making it easy for new collaborators to understand the board's geography.
3.  **Ordering the Flow:** You can drag and drop frames in the panel to change their order. This creates a linear path that you can use when presenting your work to others.

## Aligning the Team: The 'Bring to Me' Feature

One of the most frustrating experiences in virtual collaboration is the "Where are you?" conversation. You might be explaining a complex diagram, but your teammate is still zoomed out looking at the dashboard or lost in a different corner of the canvas.

To solve this, Miro uses **Followers** and the **Bring to me** command.

### Following a User
If you see a teammate's avatar (their profile picture) moving on the screen, you can click their avatar. Once you do, you are now "following" them. Your screen will automatically move and zoom wherever they go. This is ideal for when a facilitator is leading a tour of the board. To stop following, simply click anywhere on the canvas or click the "Stop following" button.

### The 'Bring to me' Command
As a facilitator or leader, you don't want to wait for people to find you. The **Bring to me** feature allows you to forcibly pull everyone's view to your current location.

**How to use it:**
1.  Click on your own avatar in the top right corner of the screen.
2.  Select **Bring everyone to me**.

Immediately, every active user on the board will have their screen snapped to exactly what you are seeing. Use this sparingly—it is a powerful tool, but "snapping" a teammate's screen while they are in the middle of typing can be disruptive.

## Navigation Scenario: The Sprint Planning Session

To see how these tools work together, let's look at a realistic scenario.

**The Setup:** Sarah is a Project Manager leading a Sprint Planning session. She has a massive board with four main sections: *Backlog*, *Prioritization*, *Task Breakdown*, and *Timeline*.

**The Workflow:**
1.  **Orientation:** Sarah starts the meeting. She notices two team members are lost. She clicks her avatar and selects **Bring everyone to me**, snapping them to the *Backlog* frame.
2.  **Guided Tour:** Sarah explains the goals. As she moves from the *Backlog* to the *Prioritization* section, the team clicks her avatar to **Follow** her, ensuring they are all looking at the same sticky notes in real-time.
3.  **Independent Work:** Sarah tells the team, "You have ten minutes to organize the *Task Breakdown* section." The team stops following Sarah. One teammate uses the **Minimap** to quickly jump over to the *Task Breakdown* area without having to pan across the entire board.
4.  **Quick Review:** After ten minutes, Sarah uses the **Frames Panel** to jump back to the *Timeline* frame to wrap up the meeting, and once again uses **Bring everyone to me** to ensure the final summary is seen by all.

## Key Takeaways

*   **Panning** (Right-click drag or Spacebar) moves you across the board; **Zooming** (Mouse wheel or +/-) changes your level of detail.
*   **Shift + 1** is the "emergency button" to zoom to all content if you get lost.
*   The **Minimap** provides a bird's-eye view and allows for "teleporting" to distant parts of the canvas.
*   **Frames** act as containers that organize content and provide a clickable table of contents in the Frames panel.
*   **Following** a user lets you see what they see; **Bring to me** pulls all collaborators to your current view.

modules.title: Core Toolset: Adding Content
modules.content:
## Your Canvas Awaits: Adding Content to the Board

Imagine this: You’re leading a brainstorming session with a global team spread across three time zones. The agenda is clear—design a new customer onboarding experience—but the ideas are scattered. Some team members have sticky notes on their physical walls, others have scattered notes in documents, and no one can see the full picture yet. You open Miro, create a board, and within minutes, everyone is adding their thoughts in real time, connecting ideas with lines, and organizing them into clear sections. The chaos of remote collaboration suddenly feels organized.

This chapter is about making that magic happen. Here, you’ll learn the core tools that turn a blank canvas into a dynamic workspace. Whether you’re documenting a process, capturing feedback, or designing a workflow, these tools are your building blocks for adding and shaping content on the board.

---

### Sticky Notes: The Building Blocks of Ideas

Sticky notes are the digital equivalent of the classic neon squares you might slap on a physical whiteboard. They’re small, flexible, and perfect for capturing quick thoughts, ideas, or tasks. In Miro, sticky notes are your go-to tool for brainstorming, organizing, or even just jotting down reminders.

#### Creating a Sticky Note
To add a sticky note to your board:
1. Look for the **Basic Toolset** on the left sidebar—this is where your most frequently used tools live.
2. Click the **Sticky Note** icon (it looks like a small yellow square with a folded corner).
3. Click anywhere on the board to place the sticky note.
4. Start typing immediately—your note is now active and ready for input.

**Tip:** If you double-click on an empty area of the board, Miro will automatically create a sticky note for you. This is a quick shortcut when you’re in the flow of capturing ideas.

#### Styling Your Sticky Note
A plain yellow sticky note is fine, but styling it helps convey meaning and makes your board more visually organized. Here’s how to customize your sticky notes:

- **Change the color**: Click on the sticky note to select it, then use the color picker in the toolbar that appears above it. Choose from Miro’s preset colors or use the custom color option to match your brand or theme.
- **Adjust the size**: Hover over any corner of the sticky note until your cursor turns into a double-headed arrow. Drag to resize the note—perfect for making it stand out or saving space.
- **Add a border**: In the toolbar, click the **Border** option to add a colored outline around your sticky note.
- **Format your text**: Use the formatting options in the toolbar to bold, italicize, or underline text. You can also change the font size or alignment (left, center, or right).

**Real-world scenario:** You’re running a workshop to redesign a website’s homepage. You ask participants to write down one feature they think is most important. After collecting 20 sticky notes, you group them by color—blue for navigation, green for content, red for calls-to-action—so you can quickly identify trends and priorities.

---

### Text Boxes: Labels, Headers, and Documentation

While sticky notes are great for quick ideas, text boxes are better suited for longer-form content, headers, or detailed documentation. Think of text boxes as the digital version of printed labels or typed notes—clean, structured, and easy to read.

#### Creating a Text Box
To add a text box:
1. Go to the **Basic Toolset** in the sidebar.
2. Click the **Text** icon (it looks like a "T" inside a box).
3. Click on the board where you want the text box to appear.
4. Start typing—your text box will expand as you add more content.

**Tip:** If you prefer keyboard shortcuts, press **T** on your keyboard to quickly activate the text tool.

#### Styling Your Text Box
Text boxes can be styled to match your needs:
- **Change the background or text color**: Use the color picker in the toolbar to adjust these settings.
- **Adjust the border**: Add or remove a border, and change its color or thickness.
- **Reshape the box**: Unlike sticky notes, text boxes can be freely resized and reshaped. Click and drag any corner to make it wider, taller, or even a different aspect ratio.
- **Add formatting**: Use the toolbar to bold, italicize, or underline text, or adjust the font size and alignment.

**Pro tip:** Use text boxes for:
- **Headers** (e.g., "Customer Feedback," "Next Steps")
- **Process documentation** (e.g., step-by-step instructions)
- **Annotations** (e.g., "Do not edit—final draft")
- **Captions** (e.g., explaining a diagram or flowchart)

**Real-world scenario:** You’re creating a user journey map in Miro. You use text boxes to label each stage of the journey (e.g., "Awareness," "Consideration," "Decision") and sticky notes to capture user pain points at each step. The text boxes provide structure, while the sticky notes add the granular details.

---

### Shapes and Connection Lines: Drawing Your Ideas

Sometimes, words aren’t enough. You need to draw boundaries, highlight sections, or show relationships between ideas. That’s where shapes and connection lines come in. They’re the tools that turn your board from a collection of text into a visual diagram.

#### Drawing Shapes
Miro offers a variety of shapes to help you visualize your ideas:
1. In the **Basic Toolset**, click the **Shape** icon (it looks like a circle inside a square).
2. A toolbar will appear with common shapes: rectangles, circles, triangles, arrows, and more.
3. Select a shape and click (or click and drag) on the board to draw it.

**Shape types and uses:**
- **Rectangles and squares**: Use for containers, process steps, or UI mockups.
- **Circles and ovals**: Great for highlighting key points or creating flowcharts.
- **Triangles**: Effective for decision points in diagrams.
- **Arrows**: Show direction or relationships between elements.
- **Clouds**: Often used in diagrams to represent "start" or "end" points.

**Styling your shapes:**
- Change the **fill color** (the inside of the shape) or **stroke color** (the outline).
- Adjust the **stroke width** (how thick the outline is).
- Add **shadows** or **rounded corners** to shapes like rectangles.

**Real-world scenario:** You’re creating a flowchart for a new feature request. You use rectangles to represent steps in the process, diamonds for decision points, and arrows to show the flow between them. The shapes make the process instantly understandable to anyone viewing the board.

#### Using the Connection Line Tool
Connection lines are the glue that holds your diagrams together. They show relationships between elements, whether it’s a sequence of steps, a cause-and-effect relationship, or a dependency between tasks.

To draw a connection line:
1. In the **Basic Toolset**, click the **Connection Line** icon (it looks like a line with two dots at the ends).
2. Click on the first element you want to connect (e.g., a sticky note or shape).
3. Drag the line to the second element and click to complete the connection.

**Types of connection lines:**
- **Straight line**: The simplest connection, great for direct relationships.
- **Elbow line**: Bends at 90-degree angles, useful for avoiding clutter.
- **Curved line**: Adds a smooth bend, often used in flowcharts or mind maps.

**Styling your connection lines:**
- Change the **line color** or **thickness**.
- Add **arrows** to indicate direction.
- Use **dashed lines** to show optional or conditional relationships.

**Pro tip:** If you need to connect multiple elements, hold down the **Shift** key while drawing to create a multi-segment line. This is especially useful for complex diagrams.

**Real-world scenario:** You’re mapping out a marketing campaign. You use sticky notes for each campaign tactic (e.g., "Social Media Ads," "Email Newsletter") and connection lines to show how they feed into each other (e.g., "Social Media Ads" → "Email Newsletter"). The lines make the dependencies clear at a glance.

---

### Uploading and Manipulating Images and PDFs

A picture is worth a thousand words, and in Miro, it can also be worth a thousand sticky notes. Uploading images and PDFs lets you incorporate existing materials—whether it’s a screenshot, a diagram, or a full-page document—directly into your board. This is especially useful for workshops, presentations, or when you need to reference external materials.

#### Uploading Files
To upload an image or PDF:
1. In the **Basic Toolset**, click the **Upload** icon (it looks like a cloud with an up arrow).
2. Choose **Upload from Computer** or select a file from cloud storage (e.g., Google Drive, Dropbox).
3. Once uploaded, the file will appear on your board as a movable element.

**Supported file types:**
- Images: JPG, PNG, GIF, SVG
- Documents: PDF, PPT, DOCX

**Tip:** Drag and drop files directly onto the board from your desktop to skip the upload step.

#### Manipulating Uploaded Files
Once your file is on the board, you can manipulate it just like any other element:
- **Resize**: Click and drag the corners to make the image larger or smaller.
- **Rotate**: Hover near the top of the image until a circular arrow appears, then drag to rotate.
- **Crop**: Click on the image and use the crop tool (in the toolbar) to trim it to a specific area.
- **Layering**: Drag elements to bring them forward or send them backward. Right-click on an element to access the **Bring to Front** or **Send to Back** options.

**Real-world scenario:** You’re facilitating a workshop to redesign a mobile app. You upload a screenshot of the current app interface and use sticky notes to annotate areas for improvement. The screenshot serves as a reference point, while the sticky notes capture the team’s feedback in real time.

#### Embedding Web Content
If you need to reference a webpage, you can embed it directly into your board:
1. Click the **More Tools** icon in the sidebar (three dots).
2. Select **Embed**.
3. Paste the URL of the webpage you want to embed.
4. Miro will generate a preview of the webpage on your board.

**Note:** Embedded web content is interactive—anyone viewing the board can click links or interact with the content directly.

**Pro tip:** Use embedded content for:
- Live dashboards or reports
- Social media posts or tweets
- Videos (e.g., YouTube embeds)

---

### Putting It All Together: A Practical Example

Let’s walk through a concrete example to see how these tools work together. Imagine you’re planning a product launch and need to create a visual roadmap that your team can collaborate on.

1. **Start with a text box** for the title: "Q3 Product Launch Roadmap." Place it at the top of the board and style it with a bold font and a contrasting background color.
2. **Add sticky notes** for each major milestone: "Market Research," "Prototype Testing," "Beta Launch," "Final Release." Color-code them by department (e.g., blue for marketing, green for product).
3. **Use shapes** to create sections for each phase of the launch. For example, draw a large rectangle around the "Market Research" and "Prototype Testing" sticky notes to group them under "Pre-Launch."
4. **Draw connection lines** between the sticky notes to show the timeline and dependencies. For example, connect "Market Research" to "Prototype Testing" with an arrow labeled "Feedback."
5. **Upload a PDF** of the launch timeline document (if you have one) to provide additional context. Crop or resize it to fit neatly on the board.
6. **Add images** of product mockups or competitor examples to inspire the team. Place them alongside the sticky notes to provide visual references.

By combining these tools, you’ve created a dynamic, interactive roadmap that your team can update in real time, comment on, and reference throughout the launch process.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Sticky notes** are your go-to tool for quick ideas, brainstorming, and capturing fleeting thoughts. Customize them with colors, sizes, and borders to organize and highlight information.
- **Text boxes** are ideal for headers, documentation, and longer-form content. Style them with backgrounds, borders, and formatting to make them stand out.
- **Shapes** help you draw boundaries, create diagrams, and visualize processes. Use different shapes (rectangles, circles, arrows) to represent various elements in your workflow.
- **Connection lines** show relationships between ideas, steps, or tasks. Choose straight, elbow, or curved lines to keep your diagrams clean and easy to follow.
- **Uploading images and PDFs** lets you incorporate existing materials into your board. Manipulate them by resizing, rotating, cropping, or layering to fit your needs.
- **Embedding web content** is useful for live references, such as dashboards or social media posts. It keeps your board dynamic and up-to-date.

With these tools in your toolkit, you’re ready to transform a blank board into a collaborative workspace that captures, organizes, and communicates ideas effectively. In the next chapter, you’ll learn how to take this content and arrange it into a logical structure—making your board not just informative, but intuitive.

modules.title: Organizing and Structuring Information
modules.content:
## Why a Messy Board is a Silent Collaboration Killer

Imagine this: You’ve spent hours gathering brilliant ideas from your team on a Miro board—sticky notes sprawled everywhere, arrows crossing like highways, and important data hidden under a pile of unorganized chaos. When the team reconvenes, no one can find the key insights buried in the mess. Frustration sets in, time is wasted, and the momentum of your collaboration grinds to a halt.

A well-organized board isn’t just about aesthetics—it’s about clarity, efficiency, and ensuring that every team member can focus on what matters instead of wrestling with disarray. This chapter will show you how to transform your Miro board from a digital scrapbook into a navigable workspace where ideas flow naturally and collaboration thrives.

---

## Grouping and Ungrouping: Building Logical Clusters

When you’re working on a board, you’ll often find yourself juggling multiple objects—whether they’re sticky notes, shapes, images, or other elements. Keeping them scattered makes it easy to lose track of relationships between ideas. That’s where **grouping** comes in.

### How to Group Objects
1. **Select multiple objects**:
   - Click and drag to draw a box around the elements you want to group.
   - Or, hold **Ctrl (or Cmd on Mac)** and click each object individually to select multiple items.
2. **Group them**:
   - Right-click and choose **Group** from the context menu.
   - Alternatively, press **Ctrl+G (or Cmd+G on Mac)**.
3. **Ungroup when needed**:
   - Right-click the grouped object and select **Ungroup**.
   - Or use **Ctrl+Shift+G (or Cmd+Shift+G on Mac)**.

### Why Group?
- **Preserve relationships**: Keep related ideas together, like a set of brainstormed features or a collection of user personas.
- **Simplify movement**: Drag and resize a group as a single unit instead of moving each item separately.
- **Reduce visual noise**: Fewer floating elements make it easier to scan the board.

**Example**: Suppose you’re designing a new app feature. You might group all the sticky notes related to "User Pain Points" into one cluster, while keeping the "Potential Solutions" in another. This way, when you revisit the board, you can instantly see the structure of your thinking.

---

## Locking Elements: Preventing Accidental Chaos

One of the most frustrating moments in virtual collaboration is when a teammate—or even you—accidentally moves a critical element. Whether it’s a key diagram, a reference image, or a carefully placed frame, unintended shifts can disrupt your workflow.

### How to Lock Objects
1. Select the object you want to lock.
2. Right-click and choose **Lock** from the context menu.
3. To unlock, right-click the object and select **Unlock**.

**Pro Tip**: Use locking for:
- **Templates or frameworks** you’ve set up.
- **Reference materials** you don’t want to move.
- **Finalized content** that shouldn’t be altered during a session.

**Scenario**: You’ve created a customer journey map with arrows and annotations. Locking the map ensures no one accidentally nudges it while adding new ideas around it.

---

## Aligning and Distributing: The Power of Visual Harmony

A board with haphazardly placed elements feels chaotic and is harder to interpret. **Alignment** and **distribution** help you create a clean, professional layout where information is easy to digest.

### Alignment Tools
Miro offers several ways to align objects:
- **Quick align buttons**: Select multiple objects, then use the alignment icons in the toolbar:
  - **Align Left**: Lines up objects along their left edges.
  - **Align Center**: Centers objects vertically.
  - **Align Right**: Lines up objects along their right edges.
  - **Align Top**: Lines up objects along their top edges.
  - **Align Middle**: Centers objects horizontally.
  - **Align Bottom**: Lines up objects along their bottom edges.

- **Distribute evenly**: After aligning, you can distribute objects so they’re spaced evenly:
  - Select multiple objects.
  - Use the **Distribute Horizontally** or **Distribute Vertically** buttons in the toolbar.

### When to Use Alignment
- **Tables or grids**: Align data points in a structured format.
- **Timelines**: Ensure dates and events are evenly spaced.
- **Diagrams**: Keep flowcharts and mind maps tidy.

**Example**: You’re mapping out a project timeline. By aligning the start and end dates of each task and distributing the intervals evenly, you create a clear, scannable overview.

---

## Colors and Tags: Categorizing with Clarity

Colors and tags are your secret weapons for making information instantly recognizable. Instead of relying on memory or guesswork, you can visually categorize content so that anyone—even a newcomer—can understand the board’s structure at a glance.

### Using Colors
- **Sticky notes**: Change the color of a sticky note by selecting it and choosing a color from the toolbar.
- **Shapes and frames**: Apply colors to borders or fills to differentiate sections.
- **Consistency is key**: Stick to a color scheme for specific types of content (e.g., red for risks, green for opportunities, blue for tasks).

### Using Tags
Tags in Miro act like digital sticky labels. Here’s how to use them:
1. Select an object (e.g., a sticky note or shape).
2. Click the **Tag** icon in the toolbar.
3. Choose an existing tag or create a new one by typing a name.
4. Assign a color to the tag for quick visual identification.

**Tag Best Practices**:
- **Limit your palette**: Too many tags can overwhelm. Aim for 5-7 core tags.
- **Use tags for status**: For example, "To Review," "Approved," or "In Progress."
- **Combine with colors**: Pair tags with colors to reinforce meaning (e.g., a red "Blocked" tag).

**Scenario**: You’re running a workshop to prioritize product features. You use:
- **Colors**: Blue for "Must-Have," orange for "Nice-to-Have," gray for "Low Priority."
- **Tags**: "Needs Discussion," "Customer Requested," "High Impact."
This way, participants can quickly scan the board and understand the status of each idea.

---

## Frames: Creating Defined Workspaces

Frames are like mini-canvases within your board, allowing you to section off content into logical chunks. They’re especially useful for:
- **Breaking down complex topics** into digestible parts.
- **Creating templates** for recurring activities (e.g., retrospectives, SWOT analyses).
- **Highlighting key areas** that need attention.

### How to Use Frames
1. **Add a frame**:
   - Click the **Frame** tool in the toolbar (or press **F**).
   - Draw a rectangle around the content you want to frame.
2. **Resize and rename**:
   - Drag the edges of the frame to adjust its size.
   - Double-click the frame’s title to rename it (e.g., "User Research Findings").
3. **Move content into frames**:
   - Drag and drop existing objects into a frame, or create new content directly inside it.

**Pro Tip**: Use frames to create a "table of contents" for your board. For example:
- Frame 1: Project Overview
- Frame 2: User Personas
- Frame 3: Workflow Diagrams
- Frame 4: Next Steps

This approach makes it easy for collaborators to navigate large boards without feeling overwhelmed.

---

## Layers and Z-Index: Controlling What’s on Top

When your board gets crowded, objects can overlap, and it’s not always clear what’s in front of what. **Layers** and **z-index** (the order in which objects are stacked) help you control visibility.

### Managing Layers
1. **Bring to front**: Right-click an object and select **Bring to Front** to place it above all others.
2. **Send to back**: Right-click and choose **Send to Back** to place it below.
3. **Layer panel**: Click the **Layers** icon in the toolbar to see a list of all objects in order. Drag items up or down to reorder them.

**When to Use Layers**:
- **Overlapping diagrams**: Ensure labels or annotations stay on top of shapes.
- **Background images**: Place decorative elements behind content.
- **Interactive elements**: Keep buttons or hotspots accessible.

**Example**: You’ve added a background image of a flowchart, but the text labels are hidden behind shapes. Use the **Bring to Front** option to ensure the labels are visible.

---

## Keyboard Shortcuts: Speed Up Your Workflow

Mastering a few keyboard shortcuts can save you time and make organizing your board feel effortless. Here are the most useful ones for this chapter:

| Shortcut (Windows) | Shortcut (Mac) | Action |
|--------------------|----------------|--------|
| Ctrl+G | Cmd+G | Group selected objects |
| Ctrl+Shift+G | Cmd+Shift+G | Ungroup selected objects |
| Ctrl+L | Cmd+L | Lock selected objects |
| Ctrl+Shift+L | Cmd+Shift+L | Unlock selected objects |
| F | F | Add a new frame |
| Ctrl+[ | Cmd+[ | Send to back |
| Ctrl+] | Cmd+] | Bring to front |
| Ctrl+A | Cmd+A | Select all objects |
| Ctrl+D | Cmd+D | Duplicate selected object(s) |

**Pro Tip**: Print out this table or save it as a reference in Miro itself. The more you use these shortcuts, the more intuitive they’ll become.

---

## Real-World Example: Organizing a Product Roadmap

Let’s walk through a step-by-step example of organizing a product roadmap board in Miro.

1. **Start with a frame**:
   - Add a frame titled "Q3 Roadmap" to define the scope.
2. **Group related items**:
   - Group all features planned for Q3 into a single group.
   - Label the group "Features."
3. **Use colors for status**:
   - Color-code each feature:
     - Green: Planned
     - Yellow: In Progress
     - Red: Blocked
4. **Add tags for priority**:
   - Create tags like "High Impact," "Customer Requested," and "MVP."
5. **Align and distribute**:
   - Align all feature cards along the left edge of the frame.
   - Distribute them evenly so they’re spaced uniformly.
6. **Lock critical elements**:
   - Lock the roadmap frame and any reference images to prevent accidental movement.
7. **Add a legend**:
   - Use sticky notes to create a legend explaining the color and tag system.

**Result**: A clean, professional roadmap that anyone on the team can understand at a glance.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even with the best intentions, it’s easy to fall into traps that make your board harder to navigate. Here’s what to watch out for:

### Pitfall 1: Overusing Groups
- **Problem**: Nesting too many groups within groups can make it difficult to move or edit content.
- **Solution**: Limit grouping to 2-3 levels deep. If you need more structure, use frames or layers instead.

### Pitfall 2: Ignoring Consistency
- **Problem**: Using random colors or tags can confuse collaborators.
- **Solution**: Define a color and tag system at the start and stick to it throughout the board.

### Pitfall 3: Leaving Objects Unlocked
- **Problem**: Accidental movements during a live session can disrupt the board’s organization.
- **Solution**: Make locking a habit for any element that shouldn’t be moved.

### Pitfall 4: Overcrowding Frames
- **Problem**: Packing too much content into a single frame makes it feel cluttered.
- **Solution**: Break large sections into multiple frames or use smaller, focused frames.

### Pitfall 5: Forgetting to Name Elements
- **Problem**: Unlabeled objects force collaborators to guess their purpose.
- **Solution**: Always give frames, groups, and tags clear, descriptive names.

---

## Quick Checklist for a Clean Board

Before sharing your board with others—or before a collaboration session—run through this checklist:

1. **Group related content**: Ensure ideas that belong together are clustered.
2. **Lock critical elements**: Prevent accidental movement of important data.
3. **Align and distribute**: Create a tidy, professional layout.
4. **Use colors and tags**: Make information instantly recognizable.
5. **Frame key sections**: Break the board into logical chunks.
6. **Check layers**: Ensure important elements aren’t hidden behind others.
7. **Name everything**: Avoid vague labels like "Untitled Group" or "New Frame."
8. **Remove duplicates**: Delete any unnecessary or redundant objects.
9. **Test navigation**: Pretend you’re a newcomer. Can you find key information quickly?
10. **Save a template**: If you’ll reuse this structure, save it as a template for future projects.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Grouping and ungrouping** helps you manage multiple objects as a single unit, making it easier to move, resize, or reorganize related ideas.
- **Locking elements** prevents accidental shifts that can disrupt your board’s layout, especially during live collaboration.
- **Alignment and distribution** tools ensure your board has a clean, professional appearance, making it easier to scan and understand.
- **Colors and tags** provide visual cues that instantly categorize content, reducing cognitive load for collaborators.
- **Frames** act as mini-canvases to section off content, helping you break down complex topics into manageable chunks.
- **Layers and z-index** control the stacking order of objects, ensuring critical elements remain visible.
- **Keyboard shortcuts** speed up your workflow, making organization feel effortless.
- **Consistency is key**: Define and stick to a system for colors, tags, and naming to avoid confusion.
- **Avoid common pitfalls** like over-grouping, ignoring labels, or leaving elements unlocked.
- **Use the quick checklist** before finalizing your board to ensure it’s clean, navigable, and collaboration-ready.

modules.title: Collaborating in Real-Time
modules.content:
## Why Real-Time Collaboration Matters

Imagine you’re working on a project with a teammate across the country. One of you sketches a flowchart while the other adds sticky notes to brainstorm ideas—all at the same time. You don’t need to email files back and forth or schedule a meeting. Instead, you’re both editing the same board in Miro, seeing each other’s changes instantly. This is the power of real-time collaboration: breaking down barriers of time and distance so teams can create, discuss, and refine ideas together, as if they were in the same room.

For teams that work remotely, across time zones, or even across desks, real-time collaboration isn’t just convenient—it’s essential. It turns a static whiteboard into a dynamic workspace where decisions happen faster, feedback is immediate, and creativity flows without friction. Whether you're designing a new product, planning a marketing campaign, or mapping out a user journey, collaborating in real time saves hours of coordination and keeps everyone aligned.

In this chapter, you’ll learn how to use Miro’s built-in features to invite others, control who can edit or view your work, communicate within the board, and stay aware of your teammates’ presence—all while working together seamlessly. No prior experience needed. Let’s get started.

---

## Inviting Your Team to the Board

Collaboration begins with bringing the right people together. In Miro, you can invite team members to your board in two main ways: via a shareable link or by sending an email invitation. Both methods are simple, secure, and give you control over who can access and edit your board.

### Sharing via a Link

A **shareable link** is a quick way to invite multiple people at once, especially if they’re already using Miro. Here’s how it works:

1. **Open the Share Panel**: Click the **Share** button in the top-right corner of your board. This opens the Share panel, where you can manage access and permissions.
2. **Generate a Link**: Under **Invite people**, click **Create a shareable link**.
3. **Choose Access Level**:
   - **Can Edit**: Gives full editing rights—team members can add, move, and delete content.
   - **Can View**: Allows viewing only, ideal for stakeholders who need to see progress but not make changes.
   - **Can Comment**: Lets people add comments and reactions, but not edit the board.
4. **Copy and Share**: Click **Copy link**, then send it via chat, email, or your team’s preferred communication tool.

> 🔒 **Security Tip**: Share links are powerful, so use them wisely. Avoid posting public links in open forums. If you need to revoke access later, you can disable the link at any time from the Share panel.

### Inviting via Email

If you know the email addresses of your teammates, inviting them directly is even easier:

1. **Open the Share Panel**: Click **Share** in the top-right.
2. **Enter Email Addresses**: In the **Invite people** field, type the email address of each person you want to invite.
3. **Set Permissions**: Choose **Can Edit**, **Can View**, or **Can Comment** for each person.
4. **Add a Message (Optional)**: Include a brief note like, “Please review the user flow by Friday.”
5. **Send Invitations**: Click **Send invites**. Each person will receive an email with a direct link to the board.

> ✅ **Best Practice**: Always include a clear subject line and message when inviting via email. It helps recipients understand why they’ve been invited and what’s expected.

### Understanding Permissions

Permissions determine what someone can do on your board. Here’s a quick breakdown:

| Permission Level | What They Can Do | Best For |
|------------------|------------------|----------|
| **Can Edit** | Add, move, delete, and edit all content | Core team members, co-creators |
| **Can View** | See the board but not modify it | Stakeholders, clients, observers |
| **Can Comment** | Add comments and reactions only | Reviewers, feedback providers |

You can change permissions anytime by opening the Share panel, finding the person’s name, and selecting a new access level.

---

## Managing Visitors and Editors

Not every collaborator needs full editing rights. Some might only need to view or comment. Miro makes it easy to adjust permissions based on role and trust level.

### Adding Visitors vs. Editors

- **Visitors** are people with **Can View** or **Can Comment** access. They’re great for passive observers or those providing feedback.
- **Editors** have **Can Edit** access. They’re your core team members who build, iterate, and co-create.

> 💡 **Pro Tip**: Use **Can Comment** for silent reviewers. This keeps the board clean while allowing structured feedback.

### Limiting Access with Limited Editable Boards

If you want to share a board with many people but only allow a few to edit, use **Limited Editable Boards**. This feature lets you:

- Allow only specific people to edit.
- Prevent accidental changes by others.

To enable it:

1. Go to **Share** > **Settings** > **Permissions**.
2. Toggle on **Limited editable boards**.
3. Add the names or emails of the people who should have editing rights.

Now, only those listed can edit—the rest can only view or comment.

> 🛑 **Caution**: This setting applies to the entire board. If you need granular control over specific elements, use **frames** or **locking** instead.

---

## Communicating Within the Board

Real-time collaboration isn’t just about sharing a board—it’s about sharing ideas and feedback, even when you’re not in the same room. Miro provides two built-in tools for communication: **chat** and **comments**.

### Using the Chat Feature

The **chat panel** lets you send messages to everyone on the board in real time. It’s perfect for quick questions, updates, or coordination.

1. **Open the Chat**: Click the **chat bubble** icon in the bottom-right corner of your board.
2. **Type Your Message**: Write your note and press **Enter** to send.
3. **Mention Someone**: Use the `@` symbol followed by their name (e.g., @Alex) to notify them directly.
4. **View History**: All messages are saved, so you can scroll back to see past conversations.

> 💬 **Use Case**: “@Team—please review the wireframe in Frame 2 by 3 PM. @Jamie, your feedback on the CTA placement is critical.”

### Adding Comments to Specific Elements

While chat is great for general updates, **comments** let you give feedback on specific parts of the board. This keeps discussion tied to the content.

1. **Select an Element**: Click on a sticky note, shape, or any content item.
2. **Add a Comment**: Click the **comment icon** (a speech bubble) that appears near the element.
3. **Write and Post**: Type your feedback and press **Enter**.
4. **Reply in Thread**: Others can respond in a comment thread, making discussions organized and contextual.

> ✅ **Best Practice**: Use comments for specific feedback. Avoid vague notes like “Fix this.” Instead, say, “The button color doesn’t meet accessibility standards—let’s try #3366FF.”

### Asynchronous vs. Real-Time Feedback

Miro supports both:
- **Real-time chat and comments** for live discussions.
- **Asynchronous feedback** when teammates respond at different times.

This flexibility means you don’t have to wait for everyone to be online to move forward.

---

## Seeing Who’s on the Board (Presence Indicators)

One of the biggest challenges in remote collaboration is knowing who’s working on what. Miro solves this with **presence indicators**—visual cues that show who else is on the board and where they’re focusing.

### Tracking Collaborator Cursors

When someone joins your board, you’ll see their **cursor**—a colored dot with their name. This shows:
- Who is active on the board.
- Where they’re working in real time.

> 👀 **Example**: If you see a blue dot with “Jamie” near the top-left corner, Jamie is currently viewing or editing content there.

This feature is especially helpful in large boards where it’s easy to lose track of activity.

### Viewing Collaborator Presence

A list of active collaborators appears in the bottom-left corner of your board. It shows:
- Their profile picture.
- Their name.
- How long ago they were last active.

This panel helps you see at a glance who’s currently engaged.

> 🔔 **Tip**: If someone’s name is grayed out, they’re on the board but not currently active.

### Using Presence to Improve Coordination

- **Avoid Overlapping Work**: See where others are editing to prevent duplicate efforts.
- **Ask Questions in Real Time**: If you see someone online, ping them via chat.
- **Reassign Focus**: If the team is clustered in one area, suggest spreading out to cover more ground.

> 📌 **Scenario**: You’re mapping a customer journey. You notice three teammates are all editing sticky notes in the “Awareness” stage. You can suggest they split up or assign roles to streamline the process.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Real Collaboration Flow

Let’s walk through a realistic example of using these features in action.

**Scenario**: You’re leading a design sprint with a 5-person team spread across two time zones. Your goal is to create a user flow for a new app feature.

1. **Set Up the Board**:
   - Name your board “Mobile App Onboarding Flow.”
   - Use frames to section off stages: Sign Up, Profile Setup, First Use, Feedback.

2. **Invite the Team**:
   - Share a **Can Edit** link via Slack: “Join the board here: [link].”
   - Also, email the designers with a note: “Please draft the user flow by EOD Thursday.”

3. **Start Collaborating**:
   - Open the **chat** and say: “@Designers—let’s start in Frame 1. @Devs, review the flow once we’re done.”
   - As people join, their **cursors** appear. You see @Jamie working on the Sign-Up flow.

4. **Give Feedback**:
   - Sarah adds a sticky note: “Add a skip option for power users.”
   - You **comment** on her note: “Great idea! Let’s add it to the ‘Edge Cases’ frame for later.”
   - Alex adds a wireframe in Frame 2. You **reply in thread**: “Can we make the CTA button larger? It’s hard to tap on mobile.”

5. **Wrap Up**:
   - You notice everyone’s cursors are idle. You send a chat message: “Great progress! Let’s sync at 4 PM to review.”
   - Before leaving, you **change permissions** to **Can View** for the client, so they can see the final draft.

By using chat, comments, presence indicators, and permission controls, your team stays aligned, productive, and engaged—without ever needing to schedule a meeting.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

Even the smoothest collaboration can hit snags. Here’s how to handle a few common problems:

### “I invited someone, but they didn’t get the email.”

- **Check Spam/Junk Folder**: Sometimes invitations land there.
- **Ask if They Used the Same Email**: If they signed up with a different email, the invite won’t go through.
- **Resend the Invitation**: Go back to the Share panel and click **Resend** next to their name.

### “I can’t find the chat panel.”

- Click the **chat bubble** in the bottom-right corner. If it’s missing, refresh your browser or log out and back in.

### “I see someone’s cursor, but they’re not responding in chat.”

- They might be focusing deeply. Try mentioning them with `@` to get their attention.

### “I accidentally gave someone edit access.”

- Go to **Share** > find their name > change permissions to **Can View** or **Can Comment**.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Use **shareable links** or **email invitations** to bring teammates onto your board quickly.
- Control access with **permission levels**: Can Edit, Can View, Can Comment.
- Manage large teams with **Limited Editable Boards** to restrict editing to key members.
- Communicate directly on the board using **chat** for general updates and **comments** for specific feedback.
- Stay aware of your team’s activity with **presence indicators**—see their cursors and who’s currently online.
- Adjust permissions and permissions as needed to keep your board secure and organized.

Real-time collaboration in Miro isn’t just about sharing a screen—it’s about creating a shared space where ideas flourish and teams move faster together. Now that you know how to invite, manage, communicate, and track activity, you’re ready to turn any board into a hub of teamwork.

modules.title: Facilitating Interactive Workshops
modules.content:
## Why Timers, Votes, and Private Mode Matter

Imagine you’re leading a brainstorming session with a remote team. The energy is high, ideas are flowing—but suddenly, one teammate dominates the conversation. Others stay quiet, perhaps intimidated or simply waiting for their turn. The result? A handful of loud voices shaping the outcome, while the rest of the group disengages. This isn’t just frustrating—it’s a missed opportunity for diverse thinking.

Virtual collaboration tools like Miro aren’t just for adding sticky notes or drawing diagrams. They’re designed to **structure interactions**, ensuring everyone has a voice, decisions are transparent, and time is respected. In this chapter, you’ll learn how to use Miro’s built-in features to lead structured activities that keep participants engaged, foster consensus, and prevent groupthink—even when you’re not in the same room.

---

## Running Structured Activities with Miro’s Facilitation Tools

Miro isn’t just a blank canvas; it’s a **facilitation platform**. The tools we’ll cover next are designed to help you guide a group through a process, whether that’s a brainstorming session, a prioritization exercise, or a walkthrough of a workflow. These aren’t just "nice-to-have" features—they’re the difference between a chaotic free-for-all and a productive, inclusive session.

### Setting Up and Running a Miro Timer for Time-Boxed Activities

**Why time-boxing matters:**
Time-boxing is a technique where you allocate a fixed amount of time to a task or activity. It keeps discussions focused, prevents over-analysis, and signals to participants when to move on. Without a timer, it’s easy for a single topic to dominate, leaving other agenda items underdeveloped—or worse, cutting them short entirely.

**How to use the Miro timer:**
1. **Open the timer panel:**
   - From any board, look for the **timer icon** in the top toolbar (it looks like a clock with a play button).
   - Click it to open the timer panel.

2. **Set the duration:**
   - Enter a time in **minutes** (e.g., 5 for a quick brainstorm or 15 for a deeper discussion).
   - The timer starts automatically when you click **Start**.

3. **Control the timer:**
   - **Pause:** Click the pause button to temporarily stop the timer.
   - **Resume:** Click the play button to continue.
   - **Reset:** Click the reset button to clear the timer and start over.

4. **Share the timer with participants:**
   - The timer appears in the top-right corner of the board.
   - Participants can see it, but **only the facilitator can start, pause, or reset it**.

**Pro tip:**
- Use the timer to signal transitions between activities. For example:
  - *5 minutes:* Write down ideas individually.
  - *3 minutes:* Share highlights with the group.
  - *10 minutes:* Discuss and prioritize.

**Scenario:**
You’re leading a workshop to redesign a customer onboarding process. You’ve split the group into breakout teams and given them 10 minutes to map out the current workflow using sticky notes. The timer ensures everyone stays on track, and you can announce, *"Time’s up—let’s hear from each team!"*

---

### Using the Voting Tool to Reach Team Consensus

**Why voting matters:**
In a group setting, not all ideas are equal. Some might be brilliant but underdeveloped; others might be popular but impractical. The voting tool in Miro helps you **quantify preferences** and **prioritize options** fairly. It’s particularly useful for:
- Deciding which features to build next.
- Narrowing down ideas from a brainstorm.
- Identifying pain points in a workflow.

**How to use the voting tool:**

1. **Add items to vote on:**
   - These could be sticky notes, shapes, or even entire frames. For example, if you’re prioritizing ideas, each idea could be a sticky note.

2. **Enable voting mode:**
   - Click the **voting icon** in the top toolbar (it looks like a thumbs-up symbol).
   - A panel will appear where you can configure the vote:
     - **Votes per participant:** Set a limit (e.g., 3 votes per person).
     - **Vote color:** Choose a color for the votes (default is yellow).
     - **Show results live:** Toggle this on if you want participants to see votes as they’re cast.

3. **Participants cast their votes:**
   - Each participant clicks on the items they support. Their vote is counted immediately.
   - If you’ve limited votes per person, they’ll see a counter next to each item.

4. **Review the results:**
   - Once voting is complete, disable voting mode (click the voting icon again).
   - The items with the most votes will be visually highlighted by the vote icons.
   - Use this data to guide the discussion. For example:
     - *"The top three ideas are X, Y, and Z. Let’s discuss why these stood out."*

**Pro tips:**
- **Limit votes per person** to prevent vote-stuffing. For example, if you have 10 options and 10 participants, allow 3 votes each.
- **Use emoji reactions** alongside voting for quick feedback. For example, 👍 for support, ❤️ for favorite, or 🤔 for uncertainty.
- **Combine voting with a discussion.** After voting, ask participants to explain their top choices. This adds context to the numbers.

**Scenario:**
You’ve just finished a brainstorming session where the team generated 20 ideas for improving team communication. You enable voting mode and give each person 3 votes. After voting, the top 5 ideas are clear. You say, *"Let’s focus on these first. Who can share why they voted for [Idea #1]?"*

---

### Applying Private Mode to Prevent Groupthink During Brainstorming

**What is groupthink?**
Groupthink happens when a group prioritizes harmony and conformity over critical evaluation. It often leads to:
- Fewer unique ideas.
- Dominant voices shaping the outcome.
- Participants hesitating to share dissenting opinions.

**How Private Mode helps:**
Private Mode in Miro allows participants to work on their own **without seeing others’ contributions in real-time**. This prevents:
- **Bandwagoning:** Where people jump on the bandwagon of the first idea they see.
- **Evaluation apprehension:** The fear of being judged for "bad" ideas.
- **Social loafing:** Where some participants disengage because they assume someone else will contribute.

**How to use Private Mode:**

1. **Enable Private Mode:**
   - From the top toolbar, click the **lock icon** (it looks like a padlock).
   - Select **Enable Private Mode**.

2. **Set the duration:**
   - Choose how long Private Mode should last (e.g., 5 or 10 minutes).
   - Participants will see a countdown timer.

3. **Participants work individually:**
   - While Private Mode is active, participants can add sticky notes, draw, or move items, but they **cannot see others’ changes**.
   - This encourages independent thinking.

4. **Disable Private Mode:**
   - When the timer ends, Private Mode turns off automatically.
   - All contributions are now visible to everyone.

**Pro tips:**
- **Use Private Mode for the "diverge" phase of brainstorming.** This is when you want as many ideas as possible, without influence from others.
- **Combine with a prompt.** Give participants a clear question or challenge to focus their thinking. For example:
  *"What are 3 ways we could improve our customer support response time?"*
- **Debrief after.** Once Private Mode ends, take time to review all contributions. Ask participants to share their favorite idea or explain why they added a particular note.

**Scenario:**
You’re leading a session to generate ideas for reducing project delays. You enable Private Mode for 7 minutes and ask everyone to add sticky notes with their ideas. When Private Mode ends, the board is filled with diverse suggestions—some obvious, some creative. You say, *"Take a moment to read through all the ideas. Which one surprises you the most?"*

---

### Using Presentation Mode to Walk a Group Through a Flow

**What is Presentation Mode?**
Presentation Mode in Miro turns your board into a **slideshow**. It’s perfect for:
- Walking a group through a process or workflow.
- Guiding participants step-by-step through an activity.
- Highlighting key areas of a board without distractions.

**How to use Presentation Mode:**

1. **Set up your board:**
   - Arrange your content in a logical sequence. For example, if you’re explaining a customer journey, order the steps from awareness to purchase.

2. **Enter Presentation Mode:**
   - Click the **presentation icon** in the top toolbar (it looks like a play button inside a rectangle).
   - A sidebar will appear where you can customize your presentation.

3. **Customize the presentation:**
   - **Frames:** Select which frames (or sections) of your board to include. Frames are like slides in a presentation.
   - **Duration:** Set how long each frame should display (default is 10 seconds).
   - **Navigation:** Choose whether participants can navigate forward/backward or if the presentation is linear.

4. **Start the presentation:**
   - Click **Start Presentation**.
   - Use the arrow keys or your mouse to move between frames.

5. **Engage the group:**
   - Pause the presentation to discuss a frame in detail.
   - Use the **laser pointer** (press and hold the spacebar) to draw attention to specific areas.
   - Ask participants questions between frames to encourage interaction.

**Pro tips:**
- **Use frames to break your board into sections.** For example, one frame for the current state, another for the future state.
- **Add a "home" frame** at the start of your presentation to orient participants.
- **Combine with the timer.** For example, set a timer for 2 minutes per frame to keep the pace moving.

**Scenario:**
You’re walking a team through a new project management workflow. You enter Presentation Mode and set up frames for each stage: *Initiation → Planning → Execution → Closure*. As you present each frame, you explain the key activities and ask, *"Does this align with how your team currently works?"* Participants can see the flow clearly and provide feedback in real-time.

---

## Putting It All Together: A Sample Workshop Flow

Here’s how you might combine these tools in a **90-minute workshop** to redesign a team’s meeting process:

| Time  | Activity                     | Miro Tool Used               | Purpose                          |
|-------|------------------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------------------|
| 0:00  | **Introduction**             | Board overview                | Set context and agenda.          |
| 5:00  | **Current State Brainstorm** | Private Mode                  | Diverge: Generate ideas freely.  |
| 12:00 | **Share Ideas**              | Voting tool                   | Converge: Prioritize ideas.      |
| 25:00 | **Ideal State Discussion**   | Presentation Mode             | Walk through proposed workflow.  |
| 40:00 | **Time-Boxed Activity**      | Timer (15 min)                | Draft a new meeting agenda.      |
| 55:00 | **Consensus Building**       | Voting tool                   | Finalize the agenda.             |
| 65:00 | **Action Planning**          | Timer (10 min)                | Assign owners and next steps.    |
| 85:00 | **Wrap-Up**                  | Board snapshot                | Review outcomes and decisions.   |

**Key takeaways from this flow:**
- **Private Mode** ensured everyone contributed ideas without influence.
- **Voting** helped narrow down the best ideas objectively.
- **Presentation Mode** made it easy to walk the group through the new process.
- **Timers** kept the session on track and signaled transitions.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Even with the right tools, facilitation can go sideways. Here’s what to watch for—and how to course-correct:

### **Pitfall 1: The Timer Runs Out, but the Discussion Isn’t Over**
- **Why it happens:** Participants need more time to explore an idea or resolve a disagreement.
- **How to avoid:**
  - Set a **buffer time** in your agenda. For example, if you allocate 10 minutes for discussion, tell the group, *"We’ll spend 10 minutes here, but if we’re deep in discussion, we can extend by 5."*
  - Use the **pause button** on the timer to extend the time without resetting.

### **Pitfall 2: Voting Results Are Too Close to Call**
- **Why it happens:** The top ideas have similar vote counts, making it hard to prioritize.
- **How to avoid:**
  - **Add a tiebreaker round.** Ask participants to vote again, but this time allow only **1 vote per person**.
  - **Discuss the "why."** Sometimes, the reasoning behind votes is more important than the numbers. Ask, *"What’s the biggest benefit of [Idea A]?"*
  - **Use a weighted system.** For example, assign 3 points to the top choice, 2 to the second, and 1 to the third.

### **Pitfall 3: Participants Ignore Private Mode and Peek at Others’ Work**
- **Why it happens:** Some participants can’t resist the temptation to see what others are doing.
- **How to avoid:**
  - **Set clear expectations upfront.** Say, *"Private Mode is active for the next 5 minutes. Please resist the urge to look at others’ boards—this is your chance to think independently."*
  - **Use a visual cue.** For example, place a large sticky note on the board saying, *"Private Mode Active—Eyes on Your Own Work!"*
  - **Check in periodically.** If someone is distracted, gently remind them of the rules.

### **Pitfall 4: Presentation Mode Feels Like a Lecture**
- **Why it happens:** The facilitator talks too much, and participants disengage.
- **How to avoid:**
  - **Ask questions between frames.** For example, *"What’s one challenge you see in this step?"*
  - **Use the laser pointer** to highlight areas where you want feedback.
  - **Encourage participation.** Say, *"Turn to the person next to you and share one thing you like about this workflow."*

### **Pitfall 5: The Board Gets Overwhelming**
- **Why it happens:** Too much content is added at once, making it hard to focus.
- **How to avoid:**
  - **Use frames** to break the board into sections.
  - **Archive or hide content** that’s no longer relevant. In Miro, you can move old content to a corner of the board or create a "parking lot" frame for off-topic items.
  - **Assign a timekeeper.** Give one participant the role of monitoring the board’s complexity and suggesting when to clean up.

---

## Preparing for Your First Facilitation Session

Facilitation isn’t just about knowing the tools—it’s about **planning the experience**. Here’s a checklist to prepare for your first session:

### **Before the Session:**
1. **Define the goal.**
   - What’s the one outcome you want? For example:
     - *"Agree on the top 3 features to build next quarter."*
     - *"Map out the current customer onboarding process."*
2. **Choose your tools.**
   - Will you use Private Mode, voting, timers, or all three? Map these to your agenda.
3. **Set up the board.**
   - Create frames for each section of your agenda.
   - Add prompts or questions to guide participants.
4. **Test the tools.**
   - Practice enabling Private Mode, starting a timer, or setting up a presentation. Make sure you know where the buttons are.
5. **Assign roles (if needed).**
   - **Timekeeper:** Monitors the timer and signals transitions.
   - **Note-taker:** Captures key decisions or action items.
   - **Tech support:** Handles any Miro glitches (e.g., lost connections).

### **During the Session:**
1. **Start with a warm-up.**
   - A quick icebreaker or check-in helps participants get comfortable.
2. **Explain the process upfront.**
   - Tell participants how you’ll use Private Mode, voting, etc. Set expectations for participation.
3. **Monitor the energy.**
   - If the group is quiet, ask open-ended questions. If they’re off-track, gently refocus them.
4. **Take breaks.**
   - Virtual fatigue is real. Schedule short breaks every 20-30 minutes.

### **After the Session:**
1. **Share the board.**
   - Export the board as a PDF or PNG and email it to participants.
   - Include a summary of decisions and next steps.
2. **Follow up.**
   - Send a thank-you note with any action items.
   - Ask for feedback: *"What worked well? What could we improve next time?"*

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Timers keep activities focused.** Use them to signal transitions and prevent over-discussion.
- **Voting democratizes decisions.** It helps prioritize ideas and reach consensus transparently.
- **Private Mode unlocks creativity.** It prevents groupthink and ensures everyone’s voice is heard.
- **Presentation Mode simplifies walkthroughs.** It turns your board into a clear, step-by-step guide.
- **Facilitation is a skill.** Combine tools with structure, clear communication, and adaptability to lead effective sessions.

modules.title: Leveraging Templates and Frameworks
modules.content:
## Why Start from Scratch When You Don’t Have To?

Imagine this: You’re preparing for a product launch workshop with your team in two hours. The goal is to map out the customer journey, identify pain points, and brainstorm solutions—all on a single board. You could spend 45 minutes setting up frames, aligning text boxes, and adjusting colors to make it visually consistent. Or, you could open Miro, search for a **Customer Journey Map** template in the Miroverse, and have a fully structured board—with placeholders for key stages, sample pain points, and color-coded sections—ready to go in under 5 minutes.

The difference? **Templates and frameworks turn blank canvases into productive spaces instantly.** Whether you're planning a sprint, designing a process, or running a brainstorming session, starting with a pre-built structure saves time, ensures consistency, and reduces cognitive load. Instead of worrying about layout or design, you can focus on the *content* and the *collaboration*.

Miro isn’t just a blank canvas—it’s a library of ready-made solutions. And in this chapter, you’ll learn how to use them effectively, customize them for your needs, and even create your own reusable templates.

---

## Browsing and Installing Templates from the Miroverse

### What Is the Miroverse?

The **Miroverse** is Miro’s public library of templates, frameworks, and examples created by both Miro’s team and the broader Miro community. Think of it as an app store for virtual collaboration: you can browse, install, and adapt templates for everything from **Agile sprint planning** to **user story mapping**, **SWOT analysis**, or **retrospective templates**.

Unlike blank boards, Miroverse templates come pre-loaded with:
- **Structured frames** (e.g., columns, swimlanes, or sections)
- **Placeholder content** (e.g., prompts like “Add your ideas here”)
- **Visual styling** (e.g., consistent fonts, colors, and icons)
- **Collaboration-ready setups** (e.g., voting areas, timers, or instructions)

These templates are built to align with common **collaboration frameworks**—reusable patterns for solving specific types of problems.

### How to Access the Miroverse

1. **From your Dashboard**:
   Click the **"Templates"** button in the top toolbar (next to “Create new board”). This opens the Miroverse in a sidebar.
2. **From a New Board**:
   Click the **"Templates"** tab on the right sidebar when creating a new board.
3. **Directly via URL**:
   Visit [miro.com/templates](https://miro.com/templates) (you’ll need to log in).

> 💡 *Tip: Use the search bar to filter by use case (e.g., “brainstorming,” “retrospective”) or industry (e.g., “healthcare,” “education”).*

### Installing a Template

Once you find a template you like:
1. Click **“Use template”** (or “Open in Miro”).
2. A new board will open with the template applied.
3. You’ll see a prompt: **“Save to Board Gallery?”** Choose **“Yes”** to keep it in your personal or team gallery for future use.

> ⚠️ *Note: Some templates are created by the Miro community. Always check the author and description to ensure it fits your needs.*

### Popular Miroverse Templates for Beginners

| Template Name | Best For | Key Features |
|---------------|---------|--------------|
| **Customer Journey Map** | Mapping user experiences | Stages, emotions, pain points, and touchpoints |
| **Agile Sprint Planning** | Scrum teams | Sprint backlog, story points, velocity tracking |
| **Mind Map** | Brainstorming ideas | Central topic with branching ideas |
| **SWOT Analysis** | Strategic planning | Four quadrants: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats |
| **User Story Mapping** | Product development | User actions, epics, and features in timeline format |
| **Weekly Planner** | Personal or team time management | Time blocks, goals, and tasks |

> ✅ *Try this now*: Go to the Miroverse and install the **Customer Journey Map** template. Explore its structure—notice how it guides you through stages like “Awareness,” “Consideration,” and “Decision.”

---

## Customizing Templates to Fit Your Project

Templates give you a head start, but they’re not one-size-fits-all. The real power comes from **adapting them to your specific goal, team, and context**.

### Step 1: Assess the Template’s Purpose

Before you customize:
- **Read the description** and any included instructions.
- **Check the framework** it’s based on (e.g., Kanban, Mind Map, SWOT).
- **Identify placeholders**: Look for text like “Add your ideas here” or empty sticky notes.

> 📌 *Example*: The **Kanban template** in Miroverse has columns like “To Do,” “In Progress,” and “Done.” If your team uses a different workflow (e.g., “Backlog,” “In Review,” “Ready for QA”), you’ll want to rename them.

### Step 2: Rename, Reorganize, and Recolor

You can edit almost everything:
- **Frames and sections**: Resize, move, or delete them.
- **Text and labels**: Rename columns, update titles, or change instructions.
- **Colors and icons**: Use your brand colors or team conventions.
- **Content**: Replace placeholders with your actual ideas, tasks, or data.

> 🛠️ *Pro tip*: Use **Ctrl/Cmd + D** to duplicate elements (like sticky notes) instead of creating new ones from scratch.

### Step 3: Add Your Own Content

Templates often include generic prompts. Replace them with your specific context:
- Instead of “Add user pain point,” write “Difficulty finding the login button.”
- Instead of “Opportunity,” write “Expand to mobile app market.”

> 🧩 *Scenario*: You’re using the **SWOT Analysis** template for a marketing campaign. The original has “Strengths” and “Weaknesses.” You rename them to “Digital Marketing Strengths” and “Budget Constraints,” and fill them with relevant data.

### Step 4: Save Your Customized Version

After customizing:
1. Click the board name at the top.
2. Choose **“Rename”** to give it a clear title (e.g., “Q2 Product Launch Roadmap – Marketing Team”).
3. Click **“Share”** to send it to your team or save it to your **Board Gallery**.

> 🔁 *Why save it?* Next time you run a similar workshop, you can reuse your customized version—no need to rebuild from scratch.

---

## Creating and Saving Your Own Templates
